title: Social Media for Breweries | Craft Beer School
desc: A practical approach to brewery social media in India: what to post, how often, and why the taproom should drive the feed, not the other way round.
teaser: Most brewery social media accounts post the same can photo with a different filter. Here is what to post instead, and why.
standfirst: Social media is one of the few marketing channels not tangled up in India's alcohol advertising restrictions. This guide covers what to actually put on it.
sections: Why this channel matters more here

Because direct alcohol advertising is restricted across most Indian mass media, your own social channels carry more of the marketing weight than they would for a brewery in a market with open advertising. Read our alcohol advertising rules guide first if you have not, because it shapes what you can safely post as well as where.

That does not mean social media is unregulated. Age gating, avoiding language that encourages consumption, and keeping content out of view of anyone under the legal drinking age still apply, and platform policies add their own restrictions on top of state rules.
Post the process, not just the product

A photo of a filled glass is the least interesting thing your account can show, because every brewery posts one. What is actually rare is the process behind it: a brewer checking gravity with a hydrometer, the mash tun steaming on a cold morning, a can line running, a delivery van being loaded at 5am before the Bengaluru traffic builds.

This content is also cheaper to produce than a styled product shoot, because it already exists on your brewhouse floor. Point a phone at the real work and post it with a short, specific caption rather than a generic one. Followers who work ordinary jobs are often more curious about how something is made than about the finished object itself.

Rotate through the stages people rarely see: milling grain, pitching yeast, dry hopping, the first taste off a fresh batch before it is carbonated. Each one is a different post, and together they build a picture of the brewery that a can photo alone never can, one that a follower could not get from any other brand.

One clever post that gets shared widely does very little for a brewery if the account goes quiet again for three weeks. A steady, unremarkable posting rhythm, three or four times a week, builds a following that actually shows up at the taproom. Chasing virality usually means chasing a format that has nothing to do with your beer, and the follower it attracts rarely converts into a customer.

Keep a simple content calendar, even a shared spreadsheet, so posting does not depend on whoever remembers to open the account that day. A brewery with two people wearing ten hats each loses this channel first when nobody owns it.
Answer the questions people actually ask

Comments and messages under brewery posts are usually the same handful of questions: where can I buy this, is it available in my city, what does it pair with, when is the taproom open. Answer them quickly and in public where possible, because the answer helps the next ten people who had the same question and never typed it.

A pinned post or a link in the bio covering stockists, hours and the food menu removes most of this traffic before it reaches your inbox, and it means a comment answered once effectively answers it for everyone who scrolls past.
Working with people who already have an audience

Sending free beer to whoever has followers is not a strategy, and it rarely produces content worth the cost. Our guide to working with beer creators covers how to pick people whose actual audience matches your buyer, and what to ask for in return, so the relationship produces something you can reuse on your own channel afterwards.
Turning the feed into foot traffic

The real test of brewery social media is not follower count, it is whether people who follow the account eventually walk into the taproom. Tie your content calendar to what is actually happening on site: a new release, a live event, a seasonal beer coming off tank. Our taproom events guide and launch guide both give the feed something worth posting about, which is the actual bottleneck for most accounts, not a lack of ideas about filters or hashtags.

If a post has no connection to anything happening at the brewery this month, it is filler, and followers can tell the difference between filler and news even when they cannot articulate why.
faqs: How often should a brewery post?
Three or four times a week, consistently, does more for a brewery's account than an occasional burst of daily posts followed by weeks of silence.
Not for most posts. Process content shot on a phone usually performs better than a styled product shot, because it looks like something a follower could not have seen anywhere else.
Can we run paid ads for beer in India?
Paid promotion of alcohol is restricted in most states in ways similar to traditional advertising, so confirm with your excise department before running any paid campaign, on any platform.
